plan: Ten new items leaning on types raters find hard (rare vocabulary, restrictive clauses, a comparison-data item) plus a cross-text selection-bias item; no resubmissions pending for SAT.

passages.title: Guarded statements
passages.text: Though the senator's public statements on the trade agreement were carefully ______, leaving reporters unsure whether she supported it, her private letters, released decades later, reveal that she had opposed it from the start.

passages.title: Four-day week
passages.text:
Text 1
Several economists argue that a four-day workweek can raise productivity. They point to trials in which companies cut weekly hours by a fifth while total output stayed about the same, meaning that each hour of work produced more than before.
Text 2
A labor researcher who reviewed the same trials notes that nearly all of the participating companies were office-based firms that chose to volunteer. Firms confident that their work could be compressed, she observes, were the ones most likely to sign up.

passages.title: The baker's step
passages.text: In a short story, the narrator describes her neighbor Mrs. Okafor as someone who concealed her generosity behind a stern manner.

passages.title: Two portraits
passages.text: Of the two portraits the museum acquired last year, the one ______ in the east wing was long attributed to a little-known painter; recent analysis of its pigments suggests that it was painted by the workshop's founder herself.

passages.title: Bridge cables
passages.text: The engineers tested the bridge's cables for corrosion ______ replaced the three that showed the most wear before reopening the bridge to traffic.

passages.title: A rushed ending
passages.text: Critics argue that the novel's ending is rushed, resolving in two pages a conflict that took three hundred to build. ______ the ending's abruptness may be deliberate: the author has said she wanted readers to feel as unprepared for the resolution as the characters are.

passages.title: Return to the village
passages.text:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Teodora has returned to her childhood village after twenty years away.
She had expected the village to be smaller, the way places from childhood are said to shrink. Instead it seemed larger, emptier. The bakery where she had bought bread every morning was shuttered, and the square where children once played was now a parking lot. She walked its length twice, as though the old square might be hiding beneath the painted lines, and then stood for a long time by the fountain, the only thing she recognized, listening to its water fall the way it always had.

passages.title: Commuting modes
passages.text:
A transportation researcher compared how commuters in one city traveled to work in 2015 and 2023.
Mode | 2015 (%) | 2023 (%)
Car | 62 | 54
Bus | 18 | 15
Bicycle | 6 | 14
Walking | 14 | 17
The researcher claims that, over this period, the share of commuters who cycled grew by more percentage points than the share for any other way of commuting.

passages.title: Ancient oats
passages.text: Archaeologists have found grinding stones bearing traces of wild oat starch at a site occupied about 32,000 years ago, long before oats were domesticated. Because the starch grains show signs of having been heated before they were ground, the researchers suggest that the site's inhabitants ______

passages.title: Learning words
passages.text: Some linguists argue that young children learn new words mainly by hearing them repeated; others argue that children learn words mainly by inferring their meanings from context. A study of toddlers complicates both views: it found that repetition mattered more for learning nouns, while context mattered more for learning verbs.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: leaving reporters unsure whether she supported it
candidates.explanation: Statements that leave listeners unsure of the speaker's position are deliberately ambiguous: "equivocal."

A.rationale: Candid statements would have made her position clear, but reporters were left unsure.

C.rationale: Vehement statements are forceful and would not leave her stance in doubt.

D.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns the timing of her statements.

hints: What effect did the statements have on reporters?
candidates.remember: Let the clause after the blank define the missing word.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the labor researcher in Text 2 most likely respond to the economists' argument in Text 1?

choices.A: She would question whether the results would hold for firms that did not volunteer.
choices.B: She would argue that the trials actually showed total output falling after hours were cut.
choices.C: She would agree that the results show a four-day week raises productivity in all industries.
choices.D: She would claim that office-based firms are generally less productive than other kinds of firms.

candidates.evidence: nearly all of the participating companies were office-based firms that chose to volunteer
candidates.explanation: Text 2 raises a selection problem: the firms that volunteered may have been the ones best suited to shorter weeks, so the results may not generalize.

B.rationale: Text 2 does not dispute the trial data, only which firms took part.

C.rationale: Her point about office-based volunteers argues against generalizing to all industries.

D.rationale: She says nothing about how productive office firms are compared with others.

hints: Does Text 2 challenge the data or who was studied?

strategy.explanation: Identify Text 2's concern before reading choices.

candidates.remember: A non-representative sample limits how far results generalize.

candidates.stem: Which quotation from the story most effectively illustrates the narrator's description?

choices.A: "She rose before dawn every day to sweep her front step until it shone like glass."
choices.B: "She was famous on our street for her sharp tongue and her refusal to lend anything."
choices.C: "She scowled at the children on her step, then secretly left them warm bread each morning."
choices.D: "She baked bread most mornings and handed it out openly to anyone who asked."

candidates.evidence: concealed her generosity behind a stern manner
candidates.explanation: The description has two parts: generosity and a stern manner that hides it. Only the quotation about scowling while secretly leaving bread shows both.

A.rationale: This shows diligence, not hidden generosity or sternness.

B.rationale: This shows sternness but no generosity at all.

D.rationale: This shows generosity, but it is open rather than concealed behind a stern manner.

hints: The description has two parts. Which quotation shows both?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate quotations that show only one part.

candidates.remember: A quotation must illustrate every part of the claim.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Of the two portraits the museum acquired last year
candidates.explanation: The clause tells which of the two portraits is meant, so it is essential (restrictive) and takes no commas: "the one that hangs in the east wing was ..."

B.rationale: A comma here sets off the clause as nonessential, but the clause identifies which of the two portraits is meant; the single comma also separates the subject from its verb.

C.rationale: The comma after "hangs" splits the verb from its modifier "in the east wing."

D.rationale: "That" introduces an essential clause and is never set off by a comma.

hints: Is the clause needed to know which portrait the sentence means?

strategy.explanation: Remove the clause: is the sentence still clear?

candidates.remember: Essential clauses identify the noun: no commas.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The engineers tested the bridge's cables for corrosion
candidates.explanation: "The engineers" is the subject of both "tested" and "replaced." Two verbs sharing one subject are joined by "and" with no comma.

A.rationale: A comma before "and" is used when it joins two independent clauses; here "replaced" has no new subject, so the comma is unnecessary.

B.rationale: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "replaced the three ..." has no subject.

C.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

hints: Does the second verb have its own subject?

strategy.explanation: Check whether a new subject follows the blank.

candidates.remember: One subject + two verbs: no comma before "and."

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: the ending's abruptness may be deliberate
candidates.explanation: The second sentence offers an alternative to the critics' view: the abruptness might be intentional. "Then again" introduces a counterpoint.

A.rationale: The second sentence offers a different reading of the ending, not a similar criticism.

B.rationale: The criticism does not cause the possibility that the abruptness is deliberate.

C.rationale: The second sentence does not restate the critics' view; it offers an alternative to it.

hints: Does the second sentence agree with the critics or offer another view?
candidates.remember: Name the relationship before choosing the transition.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Teodora is relieved to find that the village is just as she remembered it.
choices.B: Teodora finds the village unsettlingly changed, though one familiar feature remains.
choices.C: Teodora realizes that the village was always smaller than she had believed.
choices.D: Teodora decides to restore the old square to the way it looked in her childhood.

candidates.explanation: The text lists changes (shuttered bakery, square turned to parking lot), shows her searching for the old square, and ends with the one unchanged thing, the fountain.

A.rationale: The shuttered bakery and paved square show that the village has changed.

C.rationale: The text says the village seemed larger, not smaller.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests she plans to restore anything.

hints: What has changed, and what has not?
candidates.remember: A main idea covers the whole text, not one detail.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's claim?

choices.A: Cycling's share more than doubled over the period, rising from 6% in 2015 to 14% in 2023.
choices.B: The share of commuters who drove fell by 8 percentage points, from 62% in 2015 to 54% in 2023.
choices.C: Cycling rose 8 percentage points (6% to 14%); walking, the only other mode that grew, rose 3.
choices.D: Walking's share rose from 14% in 2015 to 17% in 2023, an increase of 3 percentage points.

candidates.evidence: grew by more percentage points than the share for any other way of commuting
candidates.explanation: The claim compares cycling's growth with every other mode. Only walking also grew, by 3 points, so stating cycling's 8-point rise alongside walking's 3-point rise supports the claim.

A.rationale: This is true but does not compare cycling's growth with that of any other mode.

B.rationale: This describes a decline in driving, not growth in cycling compared with other modes.

D.rationale: This gives walking's growth but never compares it with cycling's.

hints: The claim is a comparison. Which choice compares?

strategy.explanation: Compute each mode's change before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Comparison claims need data on both sides of the comparison.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: processed wild oats in several steps, perhaps drying them over heat before grinding.
choices.B: had already domesticated oats far earlier than other archaeological evidence indicates.
choices.C: relied on oats as their main source of food in every season of the year.
choices.D: used the grinding stones only for nonfood materials such as mineral pigments.

candidates.evidence: show signs of having been heated before they were ground
candidates.explanation: Heating before grinding means at least two deliberate steps in preparing the oats, which the completion states.

B.rationale: The text says the oats were wild and the site predates domestication.

C.rationale: Traces on grinding stones show oats were processed, not that they were the main food.

D.rationale: The oat starch on the stones shows they were used to grind food.

hints: What do heating and then grinding together suggest?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that go beyond or contradict the evidence.

candidates.remember: A logical completion follows from the evidence without overreaching.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents a single view, offers evidence for it, and then dismisses an objection.
choices.B: It presents two competing views and then describes a finding that partly supports each.
choices.C: It describes a study and then explains why the study's methods were flawed.
choices.D: It traces how one linguist's view of word learning changed over time.

candidates.evidence: A study of toddlers complicates both views
candidates.explanation: Two views (repetition versus context) are presented, then a study finding that repetition matters more for nouns and context for verbs, partly supporting each.

A.rationale: The text presents two views and favors neither.

C.rationale: The text does not criticize the study's methods.

D.rationale: No single linguist's changing view is described.

hints: How many views appear, and what does the study do to them?
candidates.remember: Map each sentence's job, then match the sequence.
